title: Where are lists commonly used?
body: Lists are frequently used to handle multiple values in order. Most data sets consisting of multiple items—such as lists of students, scores, files, search results, or cards—can be represented as lists.
detail: With lists, you can process items one by one using a `for` loop, add new values with `append`, or count the number of items with `len`. When reading code and encountering a list, you should check the order in which the values are stored and how they are used in loops. Lists are frequently used when collecting and processing multiple values in order. You can iterate through them one by one using a loop, accumulate results using `append`, or retrieve specific elements by index.

title: The foundation of code reading is the movement of values
body: The key to understanding code is to follow the flow of values. Variables act like labels that point to values, and assignment statements redefine the value that the label points to.
detail: For example, if you encounter `x = 3` followed by `x = x + 1`, you should interpret it as first reading the previous value of `x` (3) from the right side, adding 1 to it, and then storing the result (4) back into `x`. Even as the code gets longer, writing down how the values change line by line helps stabilize your understanding of the flow. The foundation of code reading is observing the flow of values. Values are assigned to variables, conditional statements check values, loops modify values, and functions accept and return values.

title: Dict and JSON are often used together
body: You’ll encounter `dict` and JSON very frequently in real-world Python programming. A dict is a data type that stores key-value pairs, while JSON is a string format frequently used to exchange data with servers or files.

title: The difference between row["key"] and row.get("key")
body: Bracket access raises KeyError when a key is absent, which is useful for validating a required field. get returns None or a chosen default, which is convenient for optional fields. Using get everywhere can hide invalid data, so first decide whether the field is required or optional.

title: Filtering Patterns
body: A filtering pattern is a process of retaining only the values that meet certain conditions from a larger set. In Python, this is typically done by iterating through the values one by one using a `for` loop and appending them to a new list only if the `if` condition is `True`. For example, code that keeps only scores of 60 or higher from a list of scores, or code that finds only cards with short body lengths from a list of cards, is an example of filtering. When reading this pattern, it’s easier to break it down into four parts. First, identify the source list. Second, identify the name of the current value in the `for` loop. Third, see which values pass the `if` condition. Fourth, check where the values that pass the condition are stored. The result list builds up gradually as the loop progresses. A common point of confusion for beginners is assuming that values that do not meet the condition are also stored somewhere. If there is an `append` inside the `if` statement, values for which the condition is `False` will not be appended. You must also verify whether the value being appended is the entire original value, a specific field, or a transformed value. Filtering is a fundamental pattern of data processing that is very frequently used in real-world programs—for tasks such as cleaning data, narrowing down search results, creating error lists, and selecting material for review. Filtering can involve code that modifies the original data or code that creates a new result. The approach of defining `result = []` and using `result.append(x)` creates a new list. In contrast, using `remove` or `pop` on an existing list can modify the original data. It can also be written in a single line using list comprehension, such as `[x for x in items if x > 0]`. Although the syntax differs, the core concept remains the same: iterate through candidates, evaluate whether they meet the condition, and retain only the values that pass the test in the result. During code reviews, it’s also important to verify that the conditions are neither too broad nor too narrow.

It uses a `for` loop to iterate through the candidates one by one, an `if` statement to determine whether they meet the condition, and either `append` or a comprehension to build the result. When reading the code, separating the four elements—the original list, the current value, the condition, and the destination—makes it easier to see whether the condition is too broad or too narrow.

title: Normalization is the starting point for deduplication
body: Normalization applies a defined rule for whitespace, case, or representation before comparison. Because it can merge distinct originals, define domain rules first and preserve the source value. casefold may suit human-language case matching better than lower, while URLs, names, and identifiers need different rules.

title: json.loads converts a string into a data structure
body: `json.loads` is a function that converts a JSON string into a Python data structure. For example, a string like `'{"name":"A"}'` is simply a sequence of characters on its own, but when passed through `json.loads`, it becomes a dictionary from which you can retrieve values using keys, such as `row['name']`. Conversely, `json.dumps` converts a Python dictionary or list into a JSON string. In code that reads data files, it is important to distinguish between data types before and after conversion. This card is not just for memorizing word definitions; it serves as supplementary explanation to help you understand how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code. JSON is frequently used to store a single data structure, while JSONL is advantageous for storing separate JSON objects on each line. JSONL is often easier to handle when dealing with large volumes of logs or training data. When reading code, you should check whether the entire file is read at once or processed line by line in a loop.
detail: `json.loads` converts a JSON string into a Python dictionary or list, and `json.dumps` converts a Python data structure into a JSON string. JSON files often consist of a single structure, whereas JSONL stores an independent JSON object on each line. When reading the code, you must distinguish between reading the entire file at once and iterating line by line.

title: JSONL is widely used in LLM datasets.
body: JSONL stores one independent JSON value per line and supports sequential processing of large datasets. A loop can parse each line with json.loads(), but a malformed record is not repaired automatically: record its line number and decide whether to skip or stop. Also define blank-line and encoding rules.

title: Most batch scripts follow an input-processing-output structure.
body: Most batch scripts follow an input-processing-output structure. First, they read data from a file or folder; then, they transform or validate the data; and finally, they write the results to a new file or report. In Python code, a common workflow involves creating a path using `Path`, reading data with `json.loads`, processing it with `for` and `if` statements, and saving it with `write_text`. Even long scripts become much easier to read when divided into these three parts. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify how specific variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then determine whether that line is part of the input reading stage, the value modification stage, the condition evaluation stage, or the result storage or output stage. Most batch scripts can be analyzed using an input-processing-output structure. First, identify which files or data are being read; then, check what transformations and validations are performed in the middle; and finally, see where the final result is stored. If an error occurs, it becomes easier to identify the cause by breaking down the process to see where the issue occurred—whether in the input path, the processing rules, or the output permissions.

title: Breaking Down Features into Components
body: Breaking down functionality into smaller components makes the code easier to read. Even large programs are ultimately a collection of small functions that receive input, modify values, evaluate conditions, and store or output results. For example, a validation tool can be broken down into small tasks such as reading files, parsing JSON, checking required fields, and outputting errors. When reading code, you can infer the role of each component by looking at the function names, input values, and return values. This card is not meant for simply memorizing definitions; rather, it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then determine whether that line reads input, modifies a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result. Breaking down a feature into its component parts makes the code structure clearer. For example, the login feature can be broken down into small steps such as receiving input, validating it, generating a token, saving it, and refreshing the screen. When reading code, don’t just look at the names of large features; try connecting which functions handle which responsibilities, and you’ll see the maintenance flow.
detail: Breaking down functionality into individual components makes even large codebases easier to read. title: Common Risks to Look for in Code Reviews
body: During code reviews, we don’t just check whether the code runs; we also assess the risk of future issues. For example, we verify that there are no duplicate IDs, that `answer` is within `choices`, that file paths actually exist, and that the code safely halts in the event of an exception. This review perspective is important even at the beginner level. When reading code, you should look not only at input, processing, and output but also at the error messages that appear when the code fails. This card is not just for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where the concept appears, then categorize that line: is it a step that reads input, modifies a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result? During code reviews, we don’t just check whether the code works; we also assess whether it will be easy to modify later. We verify whether names are meaningful, whether functions are overloaded, whether error handling is in place, and whether there is excessive duplication. When reading code for review, it’s helpful to highlight not only the implementation results but also any risky assumptions and maintenance costs.
